A few words to know

delegated authority
Power formally given to a role or person.
legible

threshold
A level at which a different rule applies.
transactional
Related to actual financial movements.
reproduction
A new copy of a document.
primary record
An original record of the action itself.

04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

Fiona Bell's latest update concerned the document that had ended Emma's previous day's work: 'Delegated authority — September 2011'. The team had now inspected the sheet, although parts of the surviving copy were difficult to read.

Rather than naming people responsible for particular payments, the document described three positions: scheme administrator, finance manager and trust chair. It distinguished the authority to request an exceptional decision from the authority to approve it. The distinction mattered, but the document remained a statement of responsibilities rather than a record of their exercise.

'Does it identify the approvers?' Emma asked.

'Not reliably,' Fiona replied. 'There are faint initials beside two roles, but we can't establish what those marks mean.'

Emma recorded the uncertainty without attempting to decipher the marks herself. A partly legible initial was not sufficient grounds for naming an individual.

Sarah suggested that Malcolm Vale's role as chair might explain the approvals. Emma disagreed. Even if a chair possessed delegated authority, that did not establish that Malcolm had signed any particular entry. A policy assigning power and a dated authorisation were different kinds of evidence.

One paragraph specified that exceptions above a financial limit should be referred to the chair. Unfortunately, the threshold was not legible in the available copy. Nor had Fiona established whether any surviving case exceeded it. The paragraph therefore supplied a conditional rule, not a finding about the trust's transactions.

Emma returned to the document Helen Ward had shown her. It described a student's selection and made payment dependent on further checks. Helen's cousin had not authorised further disclosure of bank details. Emma would not try to match that private application to a trust entry on the basis of guesswork.

She sent Fiona a carefully limited request: could the records team obtain a clearer reproduction of the threshold, describe the categories of authorisation and determine whether a reliable count of entries existed? She did not request student names.

In the newsroom Sarah drafted a simple sequence: Request → Authorisation → Transfer → Receipt. The first two stages could be described from the rules. The latter stages still required transactional evidence. Emma added a warning that an approval might never have resulted in money leaving the account.

Shortly before closing time Fiona emailed again. An inventory note referred to a separate authorisation register, but the records team had not located it. Its existence, completeness and contents remained unknown.

'At last, a register that might have names,' Sarah said.

'Might,' Emma replied. 'And the question isn't merely who had power. It's who exercised it in a recorded case.'

Emma ended the day facing an absence precise enough to investigate: the rules identified possible authority, but the primary record of actual approvals was still missing.
